entries.clue: Brace, after Everyman's blunt (6)

annotation.definitionFit: To blunt an argument is to weaken its force, and impairing something weakens it in exactly that way.

indicatorNotes.after: 'After' puts the brace behind the other word rather than in front of it, so the second chunk is written last.

blocks.note: Everyman is the setter's own name, so 'Everyman is' is him saying I'm.
A brace of pheasants is a pair of them.

annotation.surface: Steadying yourself because the setter has just said something tactless.
annotation.walkthrough: Everyman signs these puzzles, and when he appears in a clue he is nearly always saying I or I'm about himself. 'Blunt' looks like the adjective for plain speech and is the verb that defines.

entries.clue: The memo can lower hiccups - much appreciated! (4,4,7)

annotation.definitionFit: Help that is more than welcome is help you are glad to have, which is what 'much appreciated' says of it.

indicatorNotes.hiccups: Something that hiccups keeps jolting out of its smooth run, and letters given that jolt lose the order they came in.

blocks.note: The fifteen letters of THE MEMO CAN LOWER rearranged.

annotation.surface: A circulated note that puts a stop to someone's hiccups, to general gratitude.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Hiccups' reads as the ailment the memo cures and is the word doing the shuffling. Anagrams this long hide well, because the fodder is spread across a whole sentence instead of sitting in one phrase.

entries.clue: Opposing but touching (7)

annotation.definitionFit: Voting against a motion is opposing it, and a ladder against a wall is merely touching it — one word, a stance and a contact.

blocks.note: The first definition: set in opposition to something.
The second definition: resting in contact with something.

annotation.surface: An opponent who nonetheless does something rather moving.
annotation.walkthrough: 'But' is there only to make the two senses sound like a contrast in a sentence. The second one is physical contact, not the emotional sense of touching that the surface offers.

entries.clue: Gradients grappled with; they're highly intense (3,6)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition is a description rather than a noun: 'they're' stands in for the plural answer and the rest says what those things are like.
annotation.definitionFit: Red giants are stars swollen huge at the end of their lives, burning high overhead with an output nothing on earth comes near.

indicatorNotes.grappled with: To grapple with a thing is to wrestle it about, and letters wrestled about come to rest in a different order.

blocks.note: The nine letters of GRADIENTS rearranged.

annotation.surface: A cyclist's account of a hilly route fought out slope by slope.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Gradients grappled with' reads as one phrase about hard climbing, which is why the plural noun in front of the shuffling word passes for scenery. A red giant is the late swollen phase awaiting our own sun.

entries.clue: King of music's festive tune ending in carnage (6)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition names the woman by surname and trade, while the answer is her forename alone.
annotation.definitionFit: Carole King wrote Tapestry and a shelf of sixties standards, so 'King of music' picks out the songwriter called King and leaves her first name to find.

indicatorNotes.ending in: The ending of a word is its final letter, so only the last letter of what follows is taken.

blocks.note: A carol is the tune sung at Christmas.
The last letter of carnage.

annotation.surface: A monarch of the music world whose Christmas song finishes amid slaughter.
annotation.walkthrough: 'King' is the royalty the surface wants and a surname, the trick setters play with pop stars. Six letters rather than four is the warning that a forename is wanted as well.

entries.clue: Duchesses somewhat game (5)

annotation.definitionFit: Chess is the board game of kings, queens and bishops, so 'game' names it as one of the class.

indicatorNotes.somewhat: 'Somewhat' means only part of the thing, so part of the word beside it is taken, letter for letter as written.

blocks.note: The five letters sit unbroken inside duCHESSes.

annotation.surface: Aristocratic ladies showing a certain amount of sporting spirit.
annotation.walkthrough: A word hidden inside one long word leaves no gap for the eye to catch, so 'somewhat' is the only warning. 'Game' means willing in the surface and names a pastime in the answer.

entries.clue: Stage showing, among others, Navarro's trumpet (7)

annotation.definitionFit: A rostrum is the raised platform a speaker or conductor stands on, a stage in the plain sense of somewhere to be seen from.

indicatorNotes.showing: What a thing shows is already on view, so the letters are written out in the words that follow rather than needing to be worked for.
indicatorNotes.among others: The letters wanted are sitting among other letters, which is to say inside the phrase rather than being the whole of it.

blocks.note: The seven letters run on from the tail of the name into the head of the instrument, across the apostrophe and the space.

annotation.surface: A concert bill that features, among other acts, a trumpeter named Navarro.
annotation.walkthrough: Fats Navarro was a bebop trumpeter, so name and instrument belong together and the eye slides over them. Hidden words are buried at an apostrophe more often than anywhere else.

entries.clue: Hardly ideal, what this suggests: < kind of tense (4,4,7)

annotation.definitionFit: Something less than perfect falls short of the ideal, and 'hardly ideal' is the same shortfall put as understatement.

indicatorNotes.what this suggests: 'This' is the sign printed in the clue, and what it suggests is the phrase a mathematician reads it aloud as.

blocks.note: The mathematical sign for less than, spelt out in words.
The perfect is one of the tenses a verb can be in.

annotation.walkthrough: 'Kind of tense' looks like a state of nerves and asks for a grammarian's term. The italic sign is not decoration but half the answer, to be read out as the words mathematicians say for it.

entries.clue: Chooses new recipient for frocks following study (11)

annotation.definitionFit: To readdress a parcel is to cross out the name on it and write another, which is choosing a new recipient for it.

indicatorNotes.following: What follows something comes along behind it, so the frocks are written after the other word.

blocks.note: To study a subject at a British university is to read it.
A frock is a dress.

annotation.surface: Deciding who should be sent the frocks, once the matter has been looked into.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Study' reads as the room and is wanted as a verb. The answer's double D falls exactly where the two ordinary words meet, so the join disappears once they are written out.

entries.clue: Portray, without limits, vast tale (4)

annotation.definitionFit: An epic is a long heroic narrative — the Odyssey rather than an anecdote — so 'vast tale' gives its size and its nature at once.

indicatorNotes.without limits: The limits of a word are the letters at either end of it, and without them means both of those go.

blocks.note: To portray a scene is to depict it, and the D and T at its ends are the limits taken off.

annotation.surface: Painting a subject with no restraint whatever.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Without limits' reads as the freedom the painter is being allowed and means the outer letters go. An instruction of that kind always takes exactly one letter from each end.

entries.clue: Rejected legal wrong in red (4)

annotation.definitionFit: A Trot is a Trotskyist, and British papers have used 'red' for anyone that far left since long before the Cold War.

indicatorNotes.Rejected: To reject is to throw back, and letters thrown back arrive in the opposite order.

blocks.note: A tort is the civil wrong you are sued for rather than the crime you are charged with.

annotation.surface: A claim of wrongdoing thrown out, the ruling marked in red.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Red' sits at the end of a wholly legal picture and is the definition. Trot has been newspaper shorthand for a hard-left socialist, a follower of Leon Trotsky, since the 1970s.

entries.clue: Act superior in broadcasts behind stage (3,2,4)

annotation.definitionFit: To put on airs is to behave as though you were grander than the company, which is acting superior without being it.

indicatorNotes.behind: What stands behind something comes after it, so the broadcasts are written following the other word.

blocks.note: To stage a play is to put it on.
A channel airs a programme when it broadcasts it.

annotation.surface: A performer being grand on the transmissions made from behind the scenes.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Behind stage' asks to be read as backstage, one idea about where the broadcasts come from, and the wordplay splits it to take 'stage' as a verb. The airs in the answer are affectations, not transmissions.

entries.clue: Turbine component you may see going round again (5)

annotation.definitionFit: The rotor is the bladed wheel a turbine spins, the part that actually turns while the casing stays put.

indicatorNotes.going round again: A word that goes round again comes back as itself from the far end, so there is nothing to turn over — only a symmetry to check.

blocks.note: The definition end of the clue: the spinning part inside the machine.

blocks.clueFragment: you may see going round again
blocks.note: The wordplay end: five letters reading the same from either direction, which is all the help the clue gives.

annotation.surface: A piece of a turbine that you can watch come round once more.
annotation.walkthrough: The indicator describes the thing as well as its spelling, since a rotor goes round for a living — a second meaning the setter gets free. There are no letters to assemble, only a shape to recognise.

entries.clue: Applaud heavyweight, he plays guitar (7)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition describes a man rather than naming a class, because the answer is a surname.
annotation.definitionFit: Eric Clapton is the British blues guitarist of Cream and 'Layla', so the clue identifies him by the instrument he is famous for.

blocks.note: To applaud is to clap.
A ton is the heaviest weight in everyday British use, 2,240 pounds.

annotation.surface: Cheering on a boxer in the heaviest division of all.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Heavyweight' reads as the boxing class and is wanted as a weight, plain and heavy. Clapton played with the Yardbirds and Cream before going solo.

entries.clue: Incline, cunning defence (7)

annotation.definitionFit: A rampart is the bank of earth thrown up round a fort to keep attackers out, which is defence in its oldest building sense.

blocks.note: A ramp is a slope built to be walked or wheeled up.
Art in its older sense is cunning, the sense that survives in artful.

annotation.surface: A slope and a little cleverness offered as a way of keeping attackers out.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cunning' has to be taken as a noun, the art in artful, rather than the adjective the surface wants. Ramparts are the earth banks of Iron Age hill forts, still visible as rings on English hilltops.

entries.clue: One might be first to consider backing resolution (9)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition is a sentence about the answer rather than a synonym for it, leaning on the phrase it completes.
annotation.definitionFit: A responder is whoever answers a call, and the first responder is the paramedic or officer who reaches the scene ahead of everybody else.

indicatorNotes.backing: To back a thing is to stand at its back, so this piece goes behind the other rather than inside it.

blocks.note: Res is the everyday short form of resolution, as in a screen's high res.
To ponder a question is to consider it.

annotation.surface: Somebody who may be the first to think about supporting a motion.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Backing resolution' reads as supporting a motion at a meeting, both words pulling towards the committee room, and neither is doing that job. A responder need not be an emergency worker: anyone who answers is one.

entries.clue: Biologist was kind to rock (7)

annotation.definitionFit: 'Biologist' defines by example: Richard Dawkins is the Oxford evolutionary biologist who wrote The Selfish Gene.

indicatorNotes.rock: To rock something is to shake it back and forth, and letters shaken like that will not stay in the order given.

blocks.note: The seven letters of WAS KIND rearranged.

annotation.surface: A scientist with a soft spot for rock music.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Was kind to rock' reads as one phrase about a man's taste, so the final word passes for part of it rather than the instruction it is. Dawkins coined the word meme in 1976.

entries.clue: Blue clue, like this? (4)

annotation.definitionFit: Feeling down is feeling blue, both low in spirits; and a clue running downwards in the grid is a down, which is what this one is.

blocks.note: The first definition: in low spirits.
The second definition: the kind of clue whose answer is written downwards, as this one's is.

annotation.surface: A smutty clue, of the sort you are supposedly reading now.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Blue' offers the risqué sense first and the sad one is wanted. The second definition points at the clue's own place in the grid, a self-reference Everyman allows himself once a puzzle.

entries.clue: Venerated figure and scoundrel agreed (1,6)

annotation.definitionNote: 'Agreed' is the single word of assent, which the answer supplies as a whole two-word phrase.
annotation.definitionFit: To concur is to agree, so 'I concur' is the formal way of saying agreed.

blocks.note: An icon is the painted saint venerated in Orthodox churches.
A cur is a mongrel dog and, said of a man, a scoundrel.

annotation.surface: A saint and a villain finding themselves of one mind.
annotation.walkthrough: The enumeration gives away that the answer opens with a single letter, which is nearly always I or A. 'Agreed' looks like the verb telling you what the pair did and is the definition.

entries.clue: Components of dribble where children play (7)

annotation.definitionFit: A sandpit is the sunken box of sand in a playground or garden that small children dig about in.

indicatorNotes.Components of: The components of a word are the pieces it breaks into, and here they are written out in full with the joining word left standing between them.

blocks.note: Dribble is spit, and what the clue wants is the two pieces that word is built from, written out in full with their joining word still standing between them.

annotation.surface: Whatever a dribble is made up of, found where small children are put to play.
annotation.walkthrough: Dribble is saliva here, not football and not a trickle of water. Spelling a link word out as letters is a rare trick, which is why the parts refuse to separate on a first reading.

entries.clue: Most of red wine's drunk, increasingly full of tidings (7)

annotation.definitionFit: Newsier means carrying more news, and tidings is the older word for news — a newsier bulletin has more of it.

indicatorNotes.Most of: Most of a word is all of it bar the last letter, so the word named arrives one letter short.
indicatorNotes.drunk: A drunk cannot walk a straight line, and letters in that state will not stay in the order they were handed over in.

blocks.note: RED with its last letter left off.
The word with its 's throws five more letters into the mix.

annotation.surface: Someone who has got through most of the red wine and is more and more full of gossip.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Red wine's drunk' reads as one remark about the bottle, and the setter cuts it in two so that 'most of' shortens the first word only. Tidings for news is the language of carol services.

entries.clue: The northern tree's hairy growth (4)

annotation.definitionFit: A tash is the clipped British word for a moustache, the hair grown on the upper lip.

blocks.note: Northern English speech swallows 'the' into t', as in going down t'pub, and setters take that as a plain T.
The ash is one of the commonest British trees.

annotation.surface: The hairy stuff growing on a tree somewhere up north.
annotation.walkthrough: 'The' is the word doing the work, not 'northern', which only tells you whose mouth to hear it in. Tash for moustache is British slang of the same clipped kind.

entries.clue: Is Olympic honcho going to read out agreeable message? (5)

annotation.definitionFit: Wilco is the radio operator's 'will comply', the reply that says an instruction has been heard and will be carried out.

indicatorNotes.read out: To read something out is to say it aloud, so what is wanted is the sound of the words rather than their spelling.

blocks.note: 'Is he going to' asks whether he will, and the Olympic honcho is Sebastian Coe, the British middle-distance champion who ran the London 2012 games.

annotation.surface: Wondering aloud whether the man in charge of the Olympics will announce something everyone likes.
annotation.walkthrough: The first half of the clue is one question said aloud rather than a phrase to translate piece by piece, which is why no single word of it can be traded for letters. Wilco belongs with roger and over in radio procedure.

entries.clue: Plant contraptions for the evening, involving job (9)

annotation.definitionFit: An ironworks is an industrial plant where iron is smelted and shaped, 'plant' being the factory sense rather than anything growing.

indicatorNotes.involving: Something involving another thing has it wrapped up inside, so the second chunk lands within the first rather than after it.

blocks.note: Irons are the contraptions used for the evening of creases, and the word opens after its fourth letter.
A job of work is simply work.

annotation.surface: Machines laid on for tonight, with a bit of a job bound up in them.
annotation.walkthrough: 'For the evening' looks like the time of day and means the making even of creases, which is what an iron is for. 'Plant' at the head of the clue is a factory, not a shrub.

entries.clue: Twist 21 products like this? (5)

annotation.definitionFit: Irony is the turn a story takes when things come out the opposite way round from what was intended, and a twist in the tale is exactly that.

blocks.note: 21 across is a plant, and what such a plant turns out is iron.
Adding -y to a word makes it mean 'like that thing', the way silk gives silky.

annotation.walkthrough: A cross-reference sends you to the other clue, and what is wanted there is not its answer but the metal it produces. The question mark is the setter admitting that the suffix is doing more work than usual.

entries.clue: Could you get this merry in inn? One could! (2,5,4)

annotation.definition: Could you get this merry in inn? One could!
annotation.definitionFit: Read straight, the clue asks whether drink at the pub could leave you blissfully happy and answers itself — that state of bliss is the answer.

indicatorNotes.merry: Merry is the polite word for tipsy, and nobody in that state keeps things in the order they were handed.

blocks.note: The eleven letters of INN ONE COULD rearranged.

annotation.surface: Asking whether an evening at the pub could really make somebody that happy.
annotation.walkthrough: Read it as a question with its own answer and it describes the state straight; read the same words as letters and they spell it. 'Merry' looks like part of the pub scene and is the instruction.

entries.clue: Primarily 'hardy'; elsewhere 'ample' / 'rich' / 'typically yeomanly'? (6)

annotation.definitionFit: Every quoted word is a synonym — hardy in constitution, ample in size, rich in flavour, yeomanly in bearing — so the clue defines it four times while spelling it.

indicatorNotes.Primarily: Primarily means at the start, so only the opening letter of each word named is taken.

blocks.note: The opening letters of hardy, elsewhere, ample, rich, typically and yeomanly, read in the order written.

annotation.surface: A dictionary entry setting out what a word means here and what it means elsewhere.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Elsewhere' is what makes the trick work: it joins the list of senses and hands over the letter none of the synonyms could supply. Yeomanly means sturdy and independent, after the yeomen who farmed their own English land.

entries.clue: Bloody quality that's seldom seen (6)

annotation.definitionNote: The second definition is a relative clause standing for 'something that is seldom seen', which is the other thing the answer names.
annotation.definitionFit: Rarity is how rare a thing is — of a steak, how bloody it has been left — and a rarity is the seldom-seen thing itself.

blocks.note: The first definition: the degree to which a steak is left red, its rareness.
The second definition: a thing you come across once in a blue moon.

annotation.surface: The sort of damned good workmanship you hardly ever come across nowadays.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bloody' reads first as the British intensifier, the one that makes 'quality' sound like praise, and the sense wanted is the butcher's, a steak left red in the middle. Both halves are the same noun.
